title: The EasyScan GO machine-learning microscope detects malaria with 91.1% sensitivity and 75.6% specificity against expert microscopy at 11 sites in a study that its developer funded; a second study in London with the same funder finds 88% and 89%
summary: Against expert microscopy, the EasyScan GO machine-learning microscope read 2,250 malaria blood films at 11 sites with 91.1% sensitivity and 75.6% specificity; no patient outcome was measured.
account: A multi-center observational study, carried out in 2018 and 2019, evaluated the EasyScan GO, a digital microscopy device whose convolutional-neural-network software was developed by Intellectual Ventures' Global Good Fund. Motic built its production prototype. The 11 sites were in 11 countries: Burkina Faso, Kenya, Republic of the Congo, Senegal, South Africa, Uganda, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Nepal, Thailand and Brazil. In total 2,250 Giemsa-stained blood films were read independently by expert microscopists and by the device. The study was published in Malaria Journal on 12 April 2022 (Das et al.). Diagnostic sensitivity was 91.1% (95% CI 88.9–92.7) and specificity 75.6% (73.1–78.0); with good-quality slides specificity rose to 85.1%. Species were identified accurately in 93% of P. falciparum and 92% of P. vivax samples. Parasite density estimates were within 25% of the reference in 23% of slides. The authors conclude that the device meets WHO-TDR level 2 criteria for detection and species identification and level 4 for quantification and false-positive rate. They say that all parameters were significantly affected by slide quality. They also say that the study did not evaluate performance under routine field operation. The study was funded by the Global Good Fund, which donated the devices, and six co-authors were its employees. No patient-management outcome was measured. In a second evaluation in London, published on 10 August 2023 with the same funder and software team, the authors found that EasyScan GO had 88% sensitivity and 89% specificity against expert microscopy in 1,202 samples from returned travelers. Its authors also report that the device labeled every non-falciparum infection as P. vivax and that its parasite counts fell short of WHO expert level.
purpose: Automated detection, species identification and quantification of malaria parasites in blood films to replace or support expert microscopy. The evaluated benefit (diagnostic accuracy) is that purpose.

fields.summary: Against expert microscopy, the EasyScan GO machine-learning microscope read 2,250 malaria blood films at 11 sites with 91.1% sensitivity and 75.6% specificity; no patient outcome was measured.
fields.account: A multi-center observational study, carried out in 2018 and 2019, evaluated the EasyScan GO, a digital microscopy device whose convolutional-neural-network software was developed by Intellectual Ventures' Global Good Fund. Motic built its production prototype. The 11 sites were in 11 countries: Burkina Faso, Kenya, Republic of the Congo, Senegal, South Africa, Uganda, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Nepal, Thailand and Brazil. In total 2,250 Giemsa-stained blood films were read independently by expert microscopists and by the device. The study was published in Malaria Journal on 12 April 2022 (Das et al.). Diagnostic sensitivity was 91.1% (95% CI 88.9–92.7) and specificity 75.6% (73.1–78.0); with good-quality slides specificity rose to 85.1%. Species were identified accurately in 93% of P. falciparum and 92% of P. vivax samples. Parasite density estimates were within 25% of the reference in 23% of slides. The authors conclude that the device meets WHO-TDR level 2 criteria for detection and species identification and level 4 for quantification and false-positive rate. They say that all parameters were significantly affected by slide quality. They also say that the study did not evaluate performance under routine field operation. The study was funded by the Global Good Fund, which donated the devices, and six co-authors were its employees. No patient-management outcome was measured. In a second evaluation in London, published on 10 August 2023 with the same funder and software team, the authors found that EasyScan GO had 88% sensitivity and 89% specificity against expert microscopy in 1,202 samples from returned travelers. Its authors also report that the device labeled every non-falciparum infection as P. vivax and that its parasite counts fell short of WHO expert level.
